His eyes snap onto it. For a moment he stares at his own hand. PHYSICS
GLOBAL — gravity and inertia respected. Rain runs down the outside of the windshield and is cleared by each wiper stroke. Hair and jacket fabric carry natural lag. Mass has weight; contact shadows are correct.
SEGMENT 2 — the accelerator pedal travels under the boot with normal resistance and normal throw. The car takes up load and moves off; the body settles back into the seat.
SEGMENT 4 — his upper body pitches forward and down with real effort, but none of that force arrives at the brake pedal. The car's behaviour does not change at all.
SEGMENT 5 — the brake pedal is a normal working pedal with normal travel available, and it stays at rest for one reason only: his leg supplies no force to it. The hand on the thigh presses with real force and the flesh compresses under it. The effort is visible in tendons, tremor and compressed tissue, and none of it reaches the pedal.
SEGMENT 6 — the strain against the wheel is real and the wheel gives a few degrees at most. The hand that leaves the wheel does so smoothly and without effort, in complete contrast to everything else his body is doing. It lands on the wheel rim again with real contact and grips.

CHARACTER ACTING
Everything in this clip points at the body, not at the car. He is not fighting a machine, he is fighting himself, and the audience must be able to tell the difference.

SEGMENT 1 — ETHAN, and he says nothing. This is a man at a light, and nothing is wrong. The look up at the signal is unhurried and slightly absent — he is still somewhere in the conversation that just ended. When the green comes he does not react to it so much as absorb it. One blink. His eyes come down. The point of this segment is ordinariness: this is the last moment in the film where his body simply works.
CLAMP — urgency = wrong. A troubled expression = wrong. This is a small dull moment and it must play as one.

SEGMENT 2 — a boot and a pedal, and nothing else. The performance is that there is no performance: the foot does an easy, practised, unremarkable thing. No strain, no tremor, no hesitation. The audience should not register this shot as important. It becomes important later.

SEGMENT 4 — ETHAN. The red registers first in the eyes: pupils, then the brows lifting, then the head coming forward. His jaw sets hard. His weight goes down into his leg and his shoulder drops with the effort. When nothing happens his eyes flick down toward the footwell and back up to the road — the first flicker of the wrong kind of confusion. He tries again, harder, and his breath goes short and high in the chest.
CLAMP — a scream = wrong. Wide theatrical panic = wrong. Calm concentration = wrong. This is urgency that has just met something it does not understand.

SEGMENT 5 — a foot, a leg and a hand, and no face. The performance is entirely in the tendons and in the hand on the thigh. The hand presses like someone pushing at a stuck door. The audience arrives in this frame already following his eyeline down from the previous segment, so it reads as what he is looking at.

SEGMENT 6 — ETHAN, four phases. This is the centre of the scene.
WHILE HE FIGHTS THE WHEEL — jaw clenched, neck tendons out, breath held, the whole upper body committed to turning. This is maximum effort and it is going nowhere.
WHEN THE HAND LEAVES ON ITS OWN — his face does not react for a beat, because he has not yet understood that anything happened; his shoulders are still pushing the other way. Then his eyes snap onto the hand. The change arrives in a specific order: pupils first, then the brows, then the jaw dropping open. He is looking at his own hand as at a stranger's.
ON THE LINE — the two words are spoken downward, at the hand, not at the car and not at the road.
WHEN THE HAND RETURNS — again he does not lead it; his gaze stays where the hand was for half a second and then follows it down to the wheel. He keeps pushing at the wheel with a face that has stopped being about the wheel.
CLAMP — a scream = wrong. A blank affectless face = wrong. Resignation = wrong. Any moment of calm curiosity about the hand = wrong: he is in the middle of an emergency and this is worse than the emergency.
